title: If not now, when? (Avot 1:14)
hookLine: Hillel: if I am not for myself, who is; if only for myself, what am I; if not now, when
carry: care for yourself, care beyond yourself

cards: There's a thing on your list that's been there for weeks. The call to your grandmother. The doctor's appointment.
The apology. The form. Every morning it slides to tomorrow, and tomorrow is always a better day for it.
About two thousand years ago, Hillel gave the shortest possible answer to that list. He didn't write it down; his students remembered it, and the Mishnah kept it.

It's three questions, and it may be the most quoted saying in all of Pirkei Avot. It's on posters, in speeches, and Primo Levi borrowed it for the title of a novel. The last question is only four words in English.

teach.h: IF I AM NOT FOR MYSELF, WHO?
teach.b: Here is Hillel's saying, in chapter one. If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am for myself, what am I?
And if not now, when? The first question is about responsibility. Nobody else can live your life, learn your lessons, or do your good deeds for you.
Commentators read it this way: if I don't work on myself, no one can do it in my place. It's not selfish. It's a person standing up.
The second question turns right around.

teach.h: IF ONLY FOR MYSELF, WHAT AM I?
teach.b: When I am only for myself, what am I? A person who lives only for himself shrinks. Hillel doesn't answer.

He lets the question sit there, a little uncomfortable, for you to fill in. So the first two lines hold each other in balance: stand up for yourself, and don't stop there. The third line gives both of them a deadline.
If not now, when? The Hebrew is im lo akhshav, eimatai. Akhshav is the ordinary word for now, the one people use to call a kid to dinner.
It means this minute. Some commentators add a sharper reading: now means this life, this world, while you still have time to act.
The saying works like a staircase. Care for yourself. Care beyond yourself.
Start today. Hillel, who climbed onto a roof in the snow rather than miss one lesson, knew what it meant not to wait for a better day.

how: Hillel's three questions are among the best-known lines of Pirkei Avot, studied on summer Shabbat afternoons and often quoted in Jewish teaching as a call to act without delay.

o: now, the plain everyday word for this minute
forever, a promise that never runs out
someday, when the time is finally right

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: if I am not for myself

s: Hillel said to look after yourself first and only
his second question warns that a person only for himself shrinks.
who will be for me, what am I, and when.
he leaves it hanging, and lets the listener fill it in.

games.q: a hard phone call has been on your list for three weeks. Hillel's third question is ringing in your ears. what do you do?
o: take the first small step now.
games.why: if not now, when? the saying's last word is a deadline, and it is today.

practice: Let the list in your head come up, and notice which item has waited longest, without judging yourself for it.
Then make it smaller: find the very first step, the two-minute one, like opening the email, finding the number, writing the first line. Picture yourself taking just that step.

wordCard.voice: Akhshav. Now, the ordinary word for this minute: Hillel's third question, if not now, when, and the urgency behind it.
